title: The caliph finds him
hook: Caliph Umar, sent by a dream, brings him gold, and the harper weeps at being seen (Masnavi 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Umar's story began: the old harper walked out to the graveyard and played for God alone. Your line was play for no one. What did you do with no audience? Day one hundred ninety.

Being noticed when nobody seemed to be looking can be a strange thing. The teacher who stopped you in the hall to say she'd read what you wrote. The boss who remembered the thing you did quietly months ago. A stranger who saw you were struggling and just asked. It can undo a person. Someone can hold it together for years, and one person really seeing them is what brings the tears. We left the old harper asleep on a grave, his harp for a pillow. Somebody is on the way. Today: the caliph finds him.
screen: `NOTICED WHEN NOBODY WAS LOOKING.` → `ASLEEP ON A GRAVE.` → `THE CALIPH FINDS HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's how Rumi goes on. While the harper sleeps, the caliph Umar also falls asleep, and a voice comes to him in a dream. It tells him that a servant of God is lying in the graveyard, and that he should take seven hundred gold dinars from the treasury and bring them to him. Umar gets up and goes. He walks the whole graveyard. He sees nobody but an old man asleep, and thinks, surely not him. He circles again. Still only the old man. And then it dawns on him: this is the one. So the caliph himself is standing over a worn-out musician, the kind of man people pass without a glance. Umar waits by him until he stirs. The harper opens his eyes, sees the caliph, and starts to shake. He assumes he's in trouble. Umar tells him not to be afraid. He has come with good news. God sends greetings, and this gold, and there's more when it runs out. That's when the harper breaks. He weeps, and in Rumi's telling he flings his harp down and smashes it, crying out that it had stood between him and God. He mourns all the years he'd spent performing. The gold barely matters. What undoes him is that he was seen. Sufi readers take the heart of the story to be this: the one nobody wanted, playing to empty graves, had an audience after all. Your line: you were seen.
screen: `A DREAM, AND SEVEN HUNDRED DINARS.` · `SURELY NOT HIM.` · `THE HARPER SHAKES, THEN WEEPS.` · then, large: `YOU WERE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see someone overlooked. Settle, and let someone come to mind who gets passed by. The person who cleans the building, the quiet cousin, the neighbor who lives alone, an older relative who doesn't get many calls. Hold them in mind for a while, with no plan. Just see them, the way Umar finally saw the old man on the grave. If you pray, you can hold them there too. The bell holds the time.
Khalifa. The Arabic word for caliph, the leader of the Muslim community; Umar, who found the old harper, was the second. Today's word.
Your line: you were seen. Today, let the person you thought of know it: a message, a thank-you, or just saying their name and meaning it. Day one hundred ninety.

howItsDone: In Sufi teaching, stories like this one are read as a picture of God noticing the forgotten, and many readers take it as a reason to look for the people others pass by.

fork.setup: you're Umar. a dream sent you to find God's servant in the graveyard, and all you can find is an old harper asleep on a grave. what do you do?
options: decide the dream was wrong and go home.
keep searching for someone more respectable.
realize he is the one, and wait beside him.
fork.reveal: after circling twice, Umar understands the old musician is the one, and waits for him to wake.

original.note: Persian, from Arabic khalifa: the caliph, the leader of the Muslim community. Umar was the second.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rich man gives a poor man money.
what it means: the forgotten old man had an audience all along, and being seen is what breaks him open.
what a scholar hears: Rumi pairing the caliph Umar, famous in tradition for strictness, with a harper, whose music some jurists frowned on, and making Umar the messenger of mercy.

sources.ref: Masnavi Book 1 (the old harper: Umar's dream and the graveyard)

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: hook no longer opens 'You probably know the feeling' or tells the listener what they feel; 'the most powerful man in the city' and the aside about 'pious people' passing him by removed.

Confirm from Nicholson: Umar's dream, the voice, seven hundred dinars from the treasury, circling the graveyard, the harper trembling on waking, 'God sends greetings' and the promise of more when it runs out.
Confirm that the harper smashes his harp in Rumi's telling and calls it a veil between him and God.

Trapdoor floor 3: 'Umar, famous in tradition for strictness' and 'music some jurists frowned on' are general claims; confirm they are fair and don't read as a judgment on either. Umar is honored in Sunni tradition and viewed differently in Shia tradition; the script names him only as the caliph.
